Forecast Discussion

An upper level low in the eastern Great Lakes slowly moves to central and eastern NY state through tomorrow. The circulation around the low drives a cold front through here this evening. Ahead of the front, it remains warm and humid. A line of strong thunderstorms in southern WV is moving southeast towards our area; likely affecting us mid to late morning. The line will weaken some as it gets into the southern Appalachians but some of the storms will be on the strong side with gusty winds, heavy rain and maybe small hail.

There should be a break before more storms (strong storms possible once again) develop in the afternoon and evening. Winds are gusty much of the afternoon Tuesday.

Behind the front, cooler and drier air settles in tonight. Under high pressure, Wednesday through Friday look pleasant with comfortable temperatures and dry air (for July), although the winds are a bit gusty.

Summer begins to return Saturday as the front stalls to the south and begins to move north as a warm front. It is warmer and more humid with afternoon and evening thunderstorms possible. Some of our models are dry Saturday and some have afternoon and evening showers and thunderstorms scattered around. We'll ride the fence for now and hopefully, it becomes more clear over the next few days.

An upper level low over western TN helps generate a wave of low pressure along a stalled front to our south bringing a good chance for afternoon and evening showers and thunderstorms Sunday and Monday. Temperatures are near average but it will be quite humid.

Jul 20, 2026
Early July Heat, Revisited
Update: Summer Is Hot

We're not breaking any news here: it gets pretty hot in the summer around these parts. In the Foothills, 90s are quite common. The Hickory Airport has recorded 16 highs of 90F or greater from June 1st to July 15th, and the majority of the sub-90F days are in the mid and upper 80s. When you average out the temperatures over that same period, it has been a fairly run-of-the-mill summer. At long-term climate sites in vicinity of the Southern Appalachians, mean temperatures are all within 3 degrees of average, and within a degree or two at all of the sites within the Ray's Weather coverage area.

Despite all of this relative ho-hum, the dog days of summer kicked off with a stretch of brutal heat and humidity that rivaled and exceeded several daily records across the region. By July 2nd, which was the first day that set any records, a stout upper-level ridge (often referred to in the media as a "heat dome") was positioned almost directly over the Southern Appalachians.

The map above depicts the height of the 500-millibar pressure surface, in decameters, at 7 AM on July 2nd. The aforementioned "heat dome" is indicated by the closed brown circle over our region, with a 594 decameter contour. Any time we have abnormally high 500-millibar heights, we have above normal temperatures and, generally, dry weather. This next map depicting surface weather is quite busy, but all you really need to pay attention to is the Eastern half of the country.

The looping brown contour from south Florida to east Texas and up through the Great Lakes vicinity with the two blue "H" symbols inside indicate a large area of surface high pressure dominating the eastern ~40% of the Lower 48. Surface high pressure generally promotes dry weather, and with the time of year and place of origin of this particular batch of high pressure, above normal temperatures can be expected as well.

America 250, Deep Fried

It seemed almost too perfect that America's 250th birthday would fall on a blazing hot Saturday. Take it from someone who was looking for a swimming hole that day: the lakes, creeks, and rivers of our area were about as crowded as they'll ever be, and for good reason. That cool mountain water and shady forest floor provided a refuge from the record heat of that weekend. Speaking of the records, let's dive into just how hot it got with a nice, colorful table. The McDonald's color palette was not an intentional choice, but perhaps a fitting one for America's 250th.

The red boxes indicate a new daily record high temperature was recorded at that site on that date. The yellow boxes indicate that the record was tied. We looked at 12 reliable, permanent climate sites in our area.

Unfortunately, not all of the data from one of our hottest sites (Morganton) was present. Morganton recieves the distinction of recording the hottest temperature throughout the area during this heat wave, with a blistering high of 103F on the 3rd, tying for the 4th highest temperature on record there. Records go back to 1893!

The 3rd was the peak of the heat, with only Marshall failing to reach a record high temperature. Celo and Jefferson bested previous records by an incredible 6 degrees! Mount Mitchell came within 3 degrees of the all-time record high of 81F at 6844', but the heat was not done. July 4th, 2026 was another brutally hot day, with all but 2 of the 12 listed sites breaking or tying daily records. Just about everyone in the Foothills made it to triple digits, and Wytheville's heat peaked at a blazing 97 degrees.

Another, more prominent record fell on the 4th, and that is the all-time high at Beech Mountain. Now, this does come with an asterisk: Beech Mountain's weather records only go to back to December of 1991. So, it is certainly possible there has been a temperature of 85F or higher at some point before then. But, what we have is what we have, and while it is a short period of record, 85F is the warmest temperature ever recorded on Beech.

Boone's 90s

Boone's weather reporting location has an interesting history. From New Year's Day of 1929 to May 31st, 1980, the reporting location was closer to downtown. Starting in 1980, the station was moved to the water treatment facility behind Watauga High, along the South Fork of the New River. This is not a major move in terms of distance, but there are some differences in weather in between those sites. Down along the river, the mornings will tend to be cooler in the summertime thanks to nighttime radiational cooling. Additionally, 40+ years of urban development means that Boone proper will be warmer than the water treatment facility, thanks to the urban heat island effect.

All of this is to say that downtown Boone was likely a couple of degrees warmer than the official records will state. The two 90F readings on the 3rd and 4th are the 35th and 36th instances of a 90F high temperature in all the years of Boone weather reporting, regardless of station location. Our own station on the LifeStore building off of Blowing Rock Road recorded a high of 93.0F on the 2nd, and 91.2F on the 3rd. So, the difference is minimal, but one worth considering when splitting hairs like us scientists love to do.

To most of y'all, it was just plain hot.
